item.title: Service-Defined Autonomy: Making Service Quality Computationally Actionable
item.dc:creator: Galen Robert Collins
item.description: A governance layer can evaluate organizational requirements against the capabilities of heterogeneous autonomous systems.
item.content:encoded:
Organizations deploying autonomous systems increasingly face a subtle but consequential problem: completing a task is not the same as delivering acceptable service. As robots, digital agents, and AI-driven systems take on more responsibilities, organizations must translate their service-quality expectations into requirements that autonomous systems can act upon.

The origins of Service-Defined Autonomy (SDA) trace back to research I published in 2020 on “Improving Human–Robot Interactions in Hospitality Settings.” That work examines service robots through familiar service-quality dimensions such as reliability, responsiveness, empathy, assurance, and tangibles, and explores how individual service standards can be translated into robotic functionality. The research also exposes a deeper issue. Defining good robotic service is one thing; determining whether a particular autonomous system can deliver that level of service is another.

That distinction leads to a different question: What if service-quality requirements themselves could become computationally actionable? That question became the genesis of SDA.

SDA introduces a service-quality governance layer between organizational requirements and the autonomous systems expected to carry them out (Figure 1). It addresses both the task to be performed and the service-quality standards associated with performing that task. Instead of embedding service logic separately within each robot or agent, SDA represents service requirements in a structured, machine-readable form and evaluates them against the capabilities of available systems. This allows SDA to determine, before and during execution, whether a system can perform the task while meeting the defined service standard.

A central feature of SDA is the separation of task performance from service-quality performance. An autonomous system may successfully complete its assigned task while failing to meet the service standard associated with that task, or it may meet the service-quality standard while failing to complete the task itself. In some cases, both may fail. SDA monitors these outcomes independently and can respond when either or both requirements are not met through adaptation, recovery, selection of an alternative system, or escalation to a human. This shifts the focus from a single question, “Did the system complete the task?” to two: “Did the system complete the task?” and “Did it meet the associated service-quality standard?”

Consider a hotel delivery robot assigned to deliver a guest’s order within 15 minutes. The delivery deadline itself is a service standard, one that establishes the expected level of reliability, while successful delivery represents task completion. Service quality may also depend on how the robot performs the task: whether it maintains a safe distance and speed while traveling to the guestroom, acknowledges the guest promptly, speaks at an intelligible volume and rate when using spoken communication, protects the guest’s privacy, and responds appropriately if something goes wrong. SDA represents these requirements as machine-readable service standards, evaluates them against the robot’s capabilities and current operating status, and separately monitors task completion and service-quality performance. The specific values associated with these and other service standards, including time, distance, speed, decibels, and speech rate, are illustrative rather than universal; they would be established by the organization or another governing authority and could vary according to the customer’s needs, the task, the operating environment, and applicable requirements.

The importance of this approach extends beyond a single robot or service task. Organizations increasingly operate heterogeneous environments containing robots, digital agents, AI-driven systems, and other autonomous technologies from different vendors. Each system may have different capabilities, restrictions, interfaces, and operating conditions. A vendor-neutral service-quality layer allows organizations to define service requirements independently of any individual autonomous system and apply those requirements across a changing technology environment. Rather than separately embedding and maintaining service logic within each vendor-specific system, organizations can manage service requirements through a common governance layer, reducing dependence on vendor-specific expertise and potentially accelerating deployment and adaptation. The same governance approach can also address requirements involving privacy, safety, information assurance, operational behavior, brand standards, and compliance. An autonomous system that successfully completes a task may still create risk if the manner in which it performs that task violates one of these requirements. In this model, organizational requirements can remain consistent even as the technologies used to deliver them evolve.

As autonomous systems assume a greater role in delivering services, completing tasks will not be enough. Organizations will need ways to help ensure that autonomous systems perform those tasks according to established organizational standards. SDA proposes that service quality become part of the computational architecture itself, allowing organizations to define not only what autonomous systems should do, but how well those systems should do it.

Disclosure: Generative AI was used for editorial assistance in preparing this post and to create the conceptual illustration in Figure 1 under the author’s direction. The author reviewed and approved the resulting text and figure.

Galen Robert Collins is Professor Emeritus in the W. A. Franke College of Business at Northern Arizona University, whose research includes human-robot interaction and service quality in hospitality. He is the inventor of Service-Defined Autonomy (SDA), a patent-pending architecture for making service-quality standards computationally actionable for autonomous systems.

item.title: How Human Approvals Make AI Agents More Autonomous
item.dc:creator: Kate Liapun
item.description: It’s better to have a checkpoint to gauge an agent's path to delivering complete, accurate results than to have a quick outcome that seems legitimate but is peppered with errors someone has to fish out later.
item.content:encoded:
The premise of the agentic AI argument was that humans could sit back and let AI handle repetitive tasks that were consuming someone’s time. This brought in greater efficiency and also allowed a worker to devote time and energies to tasks that required greater critical thinking and creativity. However, during my work as a data engineer at Dwelly—a U.K. proptech scaling through acquisitions—I came across a recurring issue that made me rethink my stance. 

I’d been migrating client data from older estate agencies’ CRMs to that of Dwelly. The source CRM contained two fields, “lettings negotiator” and “property manager.” In the U.K. letting market, the first refers to the person handling the rental process, while the second manages the property after it has been let. These fields existed in our target system as well, and the AI proposed to map them. Since I was privy to conversations with the agency during onboarding, I remembered hearing an explanation that these fields were filled with wrong values since they hadn’t really been in use. With that in mind, I rejected the agent’s proposed mapping and told it to proceed with the rest, which it did correctly.

Although on surface such checkpoints might seem like they are taking away an agent’s autonomy, they do the opposite because one is more comfortable with an outcome they can trust. It’s better to have a checkpoint to gauge what path the agent is on and have complete, accurate results than to have a quick outcome that seems legitimate but is peppered with errors someone has to fish out later.

What Would Have Happened Without the Checkpoint?

Let’s consider what would happen if I hadn’t intervened. The agent would have proceeded with the mapping and the agency eventually would have discovered that the “lettings negotiator” and “property manager” values were wrong. Someone would then have had to trace the issue back and clean up the consequences of that data elsewhere. Multiply this across an entire migration and one can end up with operationally useless tables. Even worse, if the mistake is not caught those values may be used to make business decisions. So the job of the data engineer would have been doubled: operate the AI agent, trace its decisions, zero in on the mistake, let it run again, then double-check once more. That makes the argument of efficiency truly redundant.

I see this failure play out across different enterprises. An AI agent is tested in isolation and it works superbly. But once it is deployed into real-time operations, it simply becomes too costly to keep up with all the supervision, refinement, and expensive reasoning, as described in a McKinsey survey report. Gartner has also predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of similar issues with rising costs, unclear value, and weak risk controls. The most thorough findings can be found in MIT’s Project NANDA, which looked at the state of AI in business and found through surveys that while AI adoption has been high, transformation has been rare because AI tools have not integrated well into existing workflows. I must rebut some of these arguments because working at a proptech, we are in fact using AI to optimize operations and enabling a sector like lettings with tech, which has allowed automation of maintenance and payments that, in turn, improve the operations of an industry notorious for its response time.

Approval Changed What I was Willing to Automate

Without a checkpoint, I would be reluctant to let the agent delete or update the mappings because the consequences of that would simply be too high. With the approval in place, anytime the agent approached a part that required business judgement, I could step in. I find this to be a more realistic and useful form of autonomy than simply allowing unrestricted action. As a recent paper on bounded autonomy makes the case, removing safeguards only creates hallucinated success whereas approval checkpoints create practical, complete results in fewer turns. They did so by creating twenty-five scenario trials spanning seven failure families. The evaluation was small and limited to the authors’ own application, so I would not generalize too far from it, but the results match what I have seen in practice: safeguards can improve the conditions under which an agent operates rather than simply slow it down.

Approval Does Only Half of the Heavy Lifting

It doesn’t all come down to an operator manually accepting or rejecting changes. The agent must operate through predefined database operations. By giving it a narrow set of tools, it can only lead to predefined outcomes that are considered safe. Therefore, an agent still has to decide from its given tool set and supply relevant values, but it cannot modify a database on its own. Even if an agent makes a bad call in this bounded architecture, it will not be catastrophic. Most agent failures are small actions that look alright  locally but cause problems elsewhere, and this is exactly where narrow tools can help us. In sum, the approval step handles the business judgment, while the tool design handles the technical boundary. I would not trust either one by itself.

The Two Different Failure Modes I was Dealing With

It’s important to distinguish the type of failure one is facing with agents. The CRM case showed me that not every case has the same cause. For example, in my case the issue was missing context. The agent could not know what the agency had told me because the information was absent from the system. Once I supplied that fact, the agent understood the correction and carried it through. 

There are also cases where there is a reasoning-capacity problem. I ran into this problem when I asked the agent to compare several rows of data across ten columns and identify the underlying pattern. It struggled and sometimes could not identify it at all. This is supported by a RelationalFactQA study on retrieving relational facts from tables which concluded that performance deteriorated as the dimensionality of the requested output increased. On more complex relational outputs, the models evaluated in the study did not exceed roughly 25% factual accuracy. Such failures can only be resolved structurally. Tasks must be narrowed down, decomposed, or followed by an independent verification pass. If a model has exceeded its reasoning capacity, it will not benefit from greater context. 

It is important to properly identify the type of failure because the conflation of them leads to bad system design. One could end up over-explaining to an agent that simply does not have the capacity to perform that task. Or one could end up over-engineering verification problems for an agent that just needed more context. In the end, automation is supposed to make operations smoother as long as we recognize what exactly we are working with.

How I Changed My Approach

As a data engineer, I used to do these mappings manually before there were AI agents. By building this agent, I saved a lot of time from repetitive tasks and could focus on other problems in the migration pipeline. But I have also become more deliberate about how much responsibility I give an agent. For the parts of the workflow where decisions can change due to business context, I always add human approval to them. I use scoped tools instead of giving the agent unfettered system access. I also recognize the type of failure problem I run into before prescribing a solution. Instead of simply pushing forward with expanding an agent’s scope, my approach is now to assess whether a system can contain the risk of an agent’s doing. This has proven to be a much more useful way for me to benefit from agentic efficiency while also ensuring the safety of the data we work with.

Disclosure: While this post is entirely written by me, I used AI to look up sources to back my data and challenge my thoughts. I assume the structure might be flagged for being similar to an output generated by an LLM. Also, most of the sources were provided to me by AI, which I then read by myself and incorporated into this post. Some sources I added on my own. 

Kate Liapun is a Data Engineer at Dwelly, a U.K. proptech group scaling through acquisition. At Dwelly, she built the system that migrates client data from legacy estate agency CRMs into the company’s platform. Her main focus is developing a reusable, AI-powered migration product designed to move customer data at the press of a button.

item.title: What Agentic AI Requires
item.dc:creator: Madhavan Babu
item.description: What is needed to move a working prototype into operation?
item.content:encoded:
While discussions around enterprise AI often begin by asking how well a prototype answers a question, the real challenge goes further beyond it. What can an agentic system do inside an organization with proper evaluation, permission control, and clear ownership? Building a demonstration that looks convincing is challenging enough, but designing a system anyone will actually run is even harder. Fluency in a demo is useful, but it does not tell an organization whether the same system can be operated day after day.

It was clear from my experience designing and operating enterprise cloud and AI platforms. I have seen agentic prototypes that look strong in a demonstration and still stall before anyone will run them. Looking at this from the point of view of an enterprise cloud architect, a natural question arises: What is needed to move a working prototype into operation? This is the same question I asked for privacy-aware healthcare AI in a previous BLOG@CACM post, now applied to agentic systems more generally.

The first point is that evaluation has to survive real inputs. Prototype tests run against selected examples. Live traffic is messy, out of scope, or simply unlike anything in the test set. A system can score well on a prepared set of prompts and still fail once ordinary users start using it. Enterprise evaluation therefore has to include factual consistency, changes in the incoming requests, and behavior under inputs for which nobody planned. The harder problem is not the first score; it is knowing, weeks later, that quality has started to fall on ordinary work. Monitoring has to continue after go-live, and teams have to notice the drop without waiting for a complaint. A one-time acceptance test is not enough.

Secondly, permission boundaries have to be set for agents that take actions. A model that answers a question and an agent that writes to enterprise systems are not the same kind of risk. Once an agent can call tools, create records, or start other workflows, the design has to say what it is allowed to do when it is wrong. Human identities and workload identities have to have narrow permissions, proper separation of duties, temporary credentials where applicable, and a full audit trail. These people and services should not have broad access simply because they sit on the same platform. High-impact actions have to go through a human approval step, and the permissions have to be reviewed when the agent is given a new tool. If the agent only replies in a conversation, a mistake stays there. If the agent can write to a system of record, the same mistake becomes an incident the business has to reverse.

Thirdly, ownership has to be decided before deployment. When an autonomous workflow produces a wrong or harmful result, responsibility has to sit with someone specific. If that is not agreed at launch, the first real incident becomes an argument about accountability instead of a fix. Model teams, platform teams, and business owners have to work as a chain of checkpoints, not as separate units. They need agreed responsibility for data, models, controls, incidents, and changes. Records help after the fact, but they do not replace a named owner. It is often the point at which many promising prototypes fail. The technology could be demonstrated, but there is no process to approve, operate, and correct it.

Thus, the takeaway is rather obvious. For agentic AI, the model is only a piece of a bigger system. A good prototype makes the solution interesting, while discipline in evaluation, permissions, and ownership make it operable. When connecting the demonstration to production, engineers have to think about these capabilities as part of the design, not as documentation. It takes some extra effort at the beginning, but it simplifies moving from a promising prototype to a system an organization is willing to run.

Disclosure: The author used an AI writing tool in drafting this post, has reviewed the text, and agrees with its conclusions.

Madhavan Babu is a senior cloud and data engineering practitioner with more than twenty-four years of experience designing and modernizing enterprise cloud, data, and AI platforms across regulated industries. An IEEE Senior Member and ACM Professional Member, he is a co-author of the Scopus-indexed study Secure Cloud-Based Medical Imaging Analytics Framework for Privacy-Aware Disease Detection Using Deep Learning and a peer reviewer for ACM Transactions on Internet Technology.

item.title: AI Helps Scholars See a Clearer Past
item.dc:creator: Samuel Greengard
item.description: AI models routinely restore, date, and geographically place ancient inscriptions, driving discoveries that were previously beyond the reach of man or machine.
item.content:encoded:
Reconstructing the past is a painstaking endeavor. Over time, memories fade, records decay, and languages go extinct. For decades, the path to enlightenment was guided solely by human expertise. Linguists and historians meticulously studied and learned symbols, alphabets, and word patterns to fill in the blanks.

AI increasingly has a say in the process. Researchers are turning to machine learning and LLMs to understand ancient tablets and documents. This includes inscriptions in Latin and ancient Greek, along with objects written in lesser-known tongues like Old Aramaic and Akkadian. Scholars are also using AI to study cuneiform, a script that spanned 3,000 years and more than a dozen languages.

“Over thousands of years, these texts have been damaged. Bits are missing. You can’t read them anymore,” said Thea Sommerschield, an assistant professor in the Department of Classics and Ancient History at Durham University in the U.K. “Restoring the missing text, dating it, and placing it in the correct historical context is important if we want to understand everyday lives and the social interactions at that time.”

Today, models like Ithaca and Aeneas—developed jointly by Google DeepMind and academic institutions—routinely restore, date, and geographically place Greek and Latin inscriptions. Paired with human epigraphers, they’re driving discoveries that would have been beyond the reach of human or machine in the past. AI is also delivering deeper insights into Akkadian and the other languages written in cuneiform, though the progress is slower.

“AI can make inscriptions much easier to read and analyze, but historical interpretation will remain a scholarly task,” said Dominik L. Michels, an associate professor of Computer Science at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) in Saudi Arabia.

Written in Stone

Tablets crack. Stone weathers. Ink fades. What endures are bits and pieces of text with gaps where words originally appeared. The languages are known—Akkadian was deciphered in the 19th century, while Greek and Latin never vanished—so the difficulty isn’t translation; it’s filling the gaps and figuring out when the text was written, where it came from, and what it meant.

Documents like contracts and agreements—which display clear patterns—are easier to interpret than abstract poems, hymns, and laments. AI recognizes kings, cities, and objects, but struggles to go “deep into the engine of the language,” said Nathan Wasserman,  a professor of Assyriology at the Institute of Archaeology of Israel’s Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Wasserman works with AI—his team is building tools to date undated tablets—but he primarily relies on statistical clustering methods that let him explain how he arrived at a finding.

There’s also a scaling problem. More than half a million cuneiform tablets reside in museum collections worldwide—letters, receipts, epics, and incantations, Wasserman said. While this sounds like an enormous archive, frontier AI models train on trillions of words, while the surviving Akkadian corpus is only about ten million words. Even Greek and Latin, the best-documented ancient languages, fall short of the text volume needed for machine learning and LLMs, said Yannis Assael, Senior Staff Research Scientist at Google DeepMind.

Finally, there’s the script itself. For example, Akkadian uses roughly 600 signs. It isn’t the volume of signs that’s the problem; it’s polyvalence. A single sign can represent a syllable or a word. In addition, there’s no rigid orthography in Akkadian; the same word—king, for example—can be written several ways. A human familiar with the corpus can easily resolve differences; a model can only learn from examples it has seen.

By the Letter

Nevertheless, AI is making its mark. At Germany’s LMU Munich, the Electronic Babylonian Library is digitizing cuneiform fragments held in museums around the world and using AI to identify which pieces belong together. In 2025, the platform matched thirty manuscripts to a 250-line hymn praising Babylon that had been lost for 1,000 years. It’s a process that “would formerly have taken decades” without AI, said Enrique Jiménez, a professor of Ancient Near Eastern Literatures at LMU’s Institute of Assyriology.

The project involves cameras as well as algorithms. Jiménez’s team has photographed roughly 40,000 of an estimated 120,000 tablets in the British Museum over the past eight years, with similar efforts underway at museums in the U.S. and Iraq. Students hand-tagged signs on the images, building a library of roughly 160,000 cuneiform signs that hadn’t previously existed. The group used it to fine-tune a text-recognition model that runs across the full photo archive. Researchers curate the results and feed them back into the system.

An algorithm identifies tablet fragments that fit together—even when they are scattered across museums and continents. Automating the tedious matching process with machine learning has paid enormous dividends. From the 19th century until 2018, scholars made about 5,000 matches; Jiménez’s team has added 2,000 since then. The group is now focusing on dating objects—the same challenge Wasserman is pursuing—but through the shape of signs, rather than statistics. “I’m not a computer scientist, I’m a philologist,” Jiménez said. “For me, the most exciting thing is to see ancient texts being reborn.”

Others are tackling equally vexing challenges. Assael and Sommerschield—part of a larger collaboration between Google DeepMind and academic institutions—have pooled their expertise in AI and classics to build a series of models. Pythia, introduced in 2019, filled in missing characters in Greek. The follow-up model, Ithaca, which went live in 2022, added dating and geographic attribution. Aeneas, introduced in July 2025, extended the approach to Latin—dating inscriptions to within thirteen years and placing them among sixty-two Roman provinces with 72% accuracy.

Aeneas can search across vast collections of Latin inscriptions and create digital fingerprints while using multimodal inputs that span text and images. It also can restore gaps in text where the missing length is unknown. The result is more than basic pattern recognition; the model ranks possibilities. This allows human epigraphers to plug in their judgment and expertise. “We’re able to obtain a probability distribution and explore different hypotheses,” Assael said.

Not only does the technology improve the quality of research, but it also expands what scholars can do. In some cases, it takes seconds to generate information that would have taken an expert many years to accomplish. “In the past, a historian would specialize in a specific period and a specific place,” Assael said. “Suddenly you give them access to all of the ancient world, in all of the years we have documented.”

Rewriting History

At KAUST, Michels is solving the opposite problem. He has developed an AI model, DeepHadad, that reconstructs the physical surface of a damaged inscription. Michels generates synthetic data by simulating how stone deteriorates: erosion, cracking, deformation, and surface wear. The AI model uses 3D scans rather than photographs to preserve depth. “Our model never tries to understand or predict what the inscription says,” he said.

Together, better scanning, synthetic data, and more capable AI are helping scholars see further into the past. In the coming years, the digital toolkit, including AI, will only continue to improve. Historians, linguists, and technologists are likely to unlock insights that had been hidden or lost. “The seeds that have been sown from past projects are likely to flourish in the years that come,” Sommerschield said. “There is growing synergy between AI and humanities.”

Samuel Greengard is an author and journalist based in West Linn, OR, USA.

item.title: Toward a Theory of Data Ecology
item.dc:creator: Raul Castro Fernandez
item.description: The data ecology potential-effect function is an analytical model that characterizes how a given allocation of data produces system-level effects in an ecosystem.
item.content:encoded:
Data increasingly shapes the world. Understanding how it does so is essential, particularly when we seek to control its effects rather than merely react to them. Yet data’s influence rarely operates through isolated uses or deliberate choices alone. Instead, it emerges from interactions among data, human and non-human agents, algorithms, social norms, and institutions, forming complex systems whose effects are often indirect, cumulative, and difficult to anticipate. Such systems become more tractable when studied through intermediate structures that capture their dominant patterns of interaction.36 Therefore, as a level of abstraction, we use the term data ecosystems: networks of agents connected by dataflows, the movements of data through which value and harm emerge at the system level. Treating ecosystems as the unit of analysis allows us to identify the principles by which data shapes outcomes and, crucially, how those outcomes can be steered through interventions, a perspective we refer to as data ecology.

Key Insights

  • Modern AI systems expose a broader problem: We are increasingly governed by data ecosystems we do not understand. These ecosystems generate value but also propagate harm in ways that are difficult to predict or control.

  • Despite these ecosystems’ importance, our ability to design them remains limited, because the mechanisms by which data produces system-level effects are poorly understood and fragmented across disciplines.

  • To make these effects explicit, we developed a model that offers a foundation for designing interventions that shape data ecosystems, rather than merely reacting to them.

In this article, we introduce a data ecology potential-effect function, an analytical model that characterizes how a given allocation of data produces system-level effects in an ecosystem. The model is defined over dataflows rather than data, and separates the instrumental value of data from value judgments about tasks. It relies on neither utility functions nor behavioral assumptions about agents, and therefore applies even when preferences are unknown, heterogeneous, or in conflict. Within this framework, interventions are mechanisms—whether legal, economic, technical, or social—that reshape dataflows in an ecosystem. By analyzing how changes in dataflows alter potential effects, data ecology provides a unified, cross-disciplinary tool for reasoning about how data shapes ecosystems.

Data ecosystems are everywhere.  We are all entangled in many data ecosystems, across digital, biological, and social domains. A conversation with a large language model (LLM) contributes feedback—through ratings and usage patterns—that shapes future model outputs. A hospital visit generates records used not only for immediate care, but also for insurance decisions.32 The transmission of genetic data through inheritance shapes populations over generations,23 while the diffusion of behaviors and norms via cultural evolution influences social structures.15 Web search engines trade behavioral data for personalization while powering advertising markets.2,40 Within organizations, employees share data to advance internal goals.10 Organizations themselves share data through regulatory reporting and commercial exchange.12 Given how profoundly these ecosystems influence our lives, we must understand their dynamics in order to shape them for the better.

Fragmented perspectives.  Scholars and practitioners have studied data because it produces consequential effects in many different settings, from markets and institutions to privacy, power, social organization, and biological systems. As a result, distinct literatures have emerged to address specific concerns: Privacy and surveillance studies examine harms from overexposure;24,26 work on surveillance capitalism analyzes how firms extract and monetize personal data;40 research on data sovereignty highlights political struggles over control;11 and studies of data markets, whether internal to firms, governmental, or socially embedded, focus on institutional and economic dynamics.10,14,19 Economic models of network effects and data externalities show how one agent’s data or participation can influence others within market or platform settings,1,4,16,17,29 while work in commons governance and science and technology studies emphasizes how hidden infrastructures shape collective outcomes.6,28 In biological systems, genetic and epigenetic data propagates across individuals, shaping population-level outcomes through cumulative and interacting effects.

The gap.  These literatures cover different facets of data ecosystems, but they do so using different abstractions and units of analysis: Economists model data as information affecting decisions or prices; legal scholars treat it as personal information, regulated input, or a governed resource; computer scientists model it as structured inputs and outputs; and researchers in science and technology studies approach it as socially situated material. Taken together, this fragmentation makes insights across domains difficult to reconcile, leaving us without a unified conceptual foundation for explaining how data shapes ecosystems.8,20 And without understanding how data affects ecosystems, we cannot design them effectively.

The data ecology framework.  The impact of data in an ecosystem depends on what data agents possess, which in turn depends on the dataflows that occur. In this article, we introduce an analytical model of the data ecology potential of an ecosystem, which characterizes the impact that a given allocation of data could exert across agents. The framework presents several qualities that enable ecosystem-level analysis:

  • Dataflows as the unit of analysis. Rather than focusing on datasets in isolation, the model analyzes how data moves among agents and how these movements determine the distribution of data across the ecosystem.

  • Separation of data and documents. The model distinguishes abstract data from the concrete documents through which it is transmitted. Documents are costly to process, and these costs influence how data propagates through the ecosystem.

  • Separation of instrumental value of data and value judgments on tasks. Data contributes instrumentally to solving tasks, while tasks carry value judgments indicating whether their outcomes benefit or harm agents.

  • Independence from utility and behavior. The potential data effect depends only on how data is allocated across agents. It does not rely on utility functions or assumptions about agent behavior, allowing analysis even when preferences are unknown, heterogeneous, or conflicting.

Grounding analysis in dataflows allows the same framework to apply across domains spanning human decision making, algorithmic systems, and biological or cultural transmission. The data ecology potential-effect function introduced here highlights several structural properties of such systems that shape how data ecosystems evolve. These properties help explain both the opportunities and limitations of existing interventions and provide guidance for designing mechanisms that more effectively reshape dataflows.

We begin by grounding the model in a definition of data and how it generates value. We then present the data ecology potential-effect function and derive several structural implications for the analysis and design of interventions in data ecosystems.

Foundations: Data and Value

How does data, whatever it is, impact the world? We can analyze specific use cases and trace the steps by which data influences outcomes. But this case-by-case approach inevitably leads to questions about generalizability. What principles extend beyond individual cases? To understand data’s broader role in ecosystems, we need an appropriate level of abstraction, which we propose here. First, we introduce conceptual distinctions that allow us to reason precisely about what data is and how it differs from the documents that carry it. Common usage blurs content and form: The same genetic findings might be stored as a PDF of a research article, a DNA sequence file, or a spreadsheet of nucleotide counts. These are three different ways (documents) of representing the same underlying representation of reality (data). In the first two sections, we adopt ideas from a systematization of data value9 that disentangles these layers. Then we define data ecosystems, the core object of study in data ecology. 

Data, information needs, and value.

Data and information.  We define data as an abstract representation of a state of nature,a meaning a condition of an aspect of reality at a given time, past, present, or future.9 For example, the temperature in a room at noon, the average age of a country’s population in the year 2000, the set of species inhabiting a coral reef today, or the grade a student will receive on an exam next week.

Value of Data

The amount of information a state of nature X carries about another state of nature Y can be expressed with mutual information, I(Y;X)=H(Y)–H(Y/X), where H(·) denotes entropy. We define the instrumental value of data X=x to the state of nature Y as V(Y;X=x)=H(Y)–H(Y/X=x), which is an instance-level interpretation of mutual information. We define the relative value of that data as V(Y;X=x|B=b)=H(Y|B=b)–H(Y|X=x,B=b), where B=b represents existing data. The relative value of data describes the marginal contribution of data X=x to knowing Y, and depends on data already in possession of the agent, B=b.

Data carries information about the states of nature it directly represents, and often about others it does not explicitly represent. For example, a variable recording room temperature also indicates whether certain species can survive there, which is a different state of nature; a DNA sequence reveals not only an individual’s genetic makeup but also information about their relatives and evolutionary history; a timestamped social media post may disclose the poster’s location and daily routine. It is possible to describe the amount of information a variable carries about another, for example, using information theory. A specific measurement of a state of nature X that takes value X=x is data. The instrumental value of data is the amount of information data X=x conveys about Y; when there exists some background data B=b, we also consider the relative instrumental value of data, which corresponds to the value of X=x for Y given the previous existence of data B=b (see “Value of Data” box).

Agent, task, and information need.  An agent is any entity capable of storing and processing data; this includes humans, bots, teams, or organizations, depending on the context.

A task is a piece of work to be performed. Agents use data to complete tasks, even though in some ecosystems agents may not possess an explicit “motivation” or even awareness of them completing tasks. For example, an antibody records data about prior infections, which the immune system uses to mount faster responses. In this example, we consider mounting a response as a task, even though we do not claim the antibody has a motivation.

Each task induces an information need, defined as the states of nature relevant to its successful completion.9 For example, deciding whether to carry an umbrella induces the information need “Is it raining?”; a robot planning a delivery needs the current location of each item; and so on.

Data that reduces uncertainty about the relevant state of nature (e.g., barometric pressure) contributes to solving the task, even if it does not provide direct access to the target state of nature. How much data helps depends on the information it carries about the needed state of nature.

Value (of data) and value judgment (of task).  Consider the statement “Data creates value by helping solve valuable tasks.” The statement uses value in two distinct ways. We distinguish:

  • The instrumental value of data, which reflects its usefulness for solving a task

  • The value judgment an agent assigns to solving that task

Suppose data X=x helps solve task t. Agent i sees solving t as desirable, while agent j sees it as harmful. The instrumental value of X=x to Y, where Y is the information need induced by t, remains the same for both agents. What differs is their value judgment.

This distinction clarifies why the effects of dataflows are inherently agent-relative, and why understanding data ecosystems requires accounting for both alignment and conflict among agents’ information needs.

Documents and costs.  A document is a representation of data in a particular medium: a PDF or spreadsheet storing survey results, a photograph capturing the same scene as a written description, or a DNA molecule encoding a genetic sequence.

Distinguishing content from form is essential because two documents may represent the same data, thus having the same value, but impose different costs—in time, effort, or attention.35 While the value of data depends on what it represents, the cost of working with a document depends on its form and the agent’s capabilities. For a human, a dense PDF table may be easier to interpret than a CSV file; for a machine, the CSV file may require cheaper extraction.

Modeling Costs

If value and cost shared a common unit, we could subtract one from the other. Since they often do not, we introduce a scaling factor β∈[–∞,1] to model the net value of a document: β=1 when there is no cost penalty, β=0 when value is exactly offset by cost, and β<0 when cost exceeds value.

We treat cost as a damping factor on value (see “Modeling Costs” box for more details): Two documents may represent the same data, yet differ in their effective value because of costs. Thus, the value of data and the value of a document are distinct.

Documents may encode either truthful data or untruthful content (referred to as Not-Data in Castro Fernandez9). Here, we focus on truthful data. Introducing untruthful content raises questions about robustness and resilience, including how false or misleading documents distort information needs, misdirect tasks, or destabilize long-run ecosystem dynamics. These phenomena are important, but they concern the ecosystem’s vulnerability to perturbations rather than the mechanisms by which data affects ecosystems. We note that data ecology provides a natural foundation for extending the analysis to resilience in future work.

Data ecosystem.  Since its origin in biology,37 the term ecosystem has been widely adopted across domains—business, technology, politics—sometimes metaphorically, sometimes rigorously. In ecology, modern definitions emphasize flows and boundaries, especially of energy and matter.22,27

In data ecology, we define data ecosystems in terms of dataflows of documents among agents, which are entities capable of storing and processing them (e.g., humans, bots, organizations). We can thus speak of a health claims ecosystem, a genome data ecosystem, or a PII ecosystem. While this is only one way to delineate ecosystems, we find that bounding systems by document flow offers a tractable and useful abstraction for modeling data’s effects.

The Data Ecology Model

Here we present the data ecology potential-effect function, P(Y,A)(n), a model of data ecology that quantifies the potential effect of data in intervention-free data ecosystems characterized by a set of agents A and set of information needs Y after n dataflows.

What does potential effect represent?   A natural approach to evaluate data’s effect would be through agents’ utilities.25 With well-defined utilities, one could use aggregated measures such as welfare as indications of “effect.” However, this approach would require access to utility functions, which are difficult or impossible to specify in many ecosystems—whether for species in a genetic environment, users in a decentralized social network, or autonomous agents with opaque goals. And it requires behavioral assumptions that often fail in practice.18,34 In contrast, potential effect applies even when agents lack explicit preferences or when those preferences are inaccessible.

We define data’s potential effect via two elements: its instrumental contribution to solving tasks, and the value judgments assigned to those tasks. First, data plays an instrumental role: It determines how much progress an agent could in principle make on the information needs induced by its tasks. This role resembles a production function in economics: Data expands an agent’s capacity to solve tasks, independent of whether that capacity is exercised. Second, tasks carry binary value judgments that indicate whether such progress would benefit or harm each agent, including potential spillovers. These judgments are not utilities: They do not describe preferences over complete outcomes, encode trade-offs, or determine choice behavior. They simply label each task as helpful or harmful. Combining the instrumental (production-like) capacity of data with these task-level judgments yields its potential effect. The term potential echoes dynamical systems: It summarizes the magnitude and direction of the effect that the current distribution of data could exert on the ecosystem. Potential effect is therefore a system-level measure of data’s latent impact, distinct from utilities and from observed outcomes.

Data ecology potential-effect function.  Before presenting the model, we must discuss dataflows and correlated data.

Dataflows.  A dataflow is the transfer of data from a source agent to a target agent, possibly transformed or derived from the source’s existing data. Dataflows may be intentional (e.g., a dataset exchange) or unintentional (e.g., overhearing, inference, or inheritance). When a target agent gains access to data it did not previously possess, that is a dataflow, no matter how the document is transmitted. Dataflows create new potential to address new tasks or to address existing tasks more effectively.

Data is correlated.  Because states of nature are correlated, data often reveals information not only about the state of nature it directly represents, but also about related states.1,3,5,33 A person’s location, genome, or preferences may be predictive of others; logs from one machine can expose the operating state of others in the same system; a water sample’s DNA can signal the presence of multiple species. Data correlations mean that dataflows cause spillover effects. These spillovers arise from structural relationships in the world, and therefore persist regardless of how data is collected or shared.

Putting it all together.  After n dataflows, each agent i holds data Bi(n). The ecosystem’s potential effect P(Y,A)(n) aggregates across agents how each agent’s data could influence (A) the agent’s own positively and negatively valued information needs and (B) spillovers on other agents’ information needs. These contributions (A and B) are moderated by processing costs: Documents are costly to interpret and differ across agents due to varying skills and resources, and evolve with what they have already received (see “Data Ecology Potential-Effect Function” box).

  Data Ecology Potential-Effect Function

Given agents A with information needs Y so that agent i’s positively valued tasks induce information needs Yi+∈Yi∈Y (and negative tasks Yi–∈Yi∈Y), and let Bi(n) denote agent i’s data after n dataflows. Then P(Y,A)(n) is given by this expression:

P ( Y , A ) ( n ) = ∑ i ∈ A β Y i + ( n ) V ( Y i + ; B i ( n ) ) – β Y i – ( n ) V ( Y i – ; B i ( n ) ) + β Y – [ i ] + ( n ) V ( Y – [ i ] + ; B i ( n ) ) – β Y – [ i ] – ( n ) V ( Y – [ i ] – ; B i ( n ) ) (1)

where βYi(n)≤1 reflects cumulative processing costs across dataflows for agent i. This expression aggregates four components per agent:

  • Positive and negative effects on the agent, Yi+, Yi– (first two terms).

  • Positive and negative spillovers on other agents, Y–[i]+, Y–[i]– (last two terms)

The value terms are positive by definition; the sign indicates whether the agent judges the task as desirable or not. Agents may use data to complete tasks with negative consequences for themselves, for example, due to bounded rationality or ignorance.

At any point in time, agents use their data—knowingly or unknowingly—to fulfill information needs (complete tasks), which yields an effect on them. Furthermore, because data is correlated, a dataflow causes effects beyond the involved source and target agents. Such effects change as dataflows take place, that is, as n increases. It is useful to consider the potential effect of an individual dataflow, which makes explicit how a single exchange can affect agents beyond those directly involved through spillover effects (see “Potential Effect of Dataflows” box).

Potential Effect of Dataflows

We define the potential effect of a single dataflow 〈s,x,t〉 as:

P s , x , t ( Y , A ) = β Y s + V ( Y s + ; X = x / B t = b t ) – β Y s – V ( Y s – ; X = x / B t = b t ) + β Y t + V ( Y t + ; X = x / B t = b t ) – β Y t – V ( Y t – ; X = x / B t = b t ) + β Y – [ s , t ] + V ( Y – [ s , t ] + ; X = x / B t = b t ) – β Y – [ s , t ] – V ( Y – [ s , t ] – ; X = x / B t = b t ) (2)

This captures the effect on source (s), target (t), and other agents (A{s,t}). Once t receives x, it integrates it into its own data Bt=bt after incurring a cost β, which indicates the cost to the target agent of processing the document that represents X=x.

Interpreting the data ecology potential-effect function.  The potential-effect function aggregates the potential effects of data across agents and information needs. The summation should be interpreted as a decomposition of effects. Nonlinearities arise from the value of the data structure of the model, which is defined using mutual information. The value terms V(Y;Bi) depend on the data already held by an agent, so the marginal contribution of a document depends on the other documents available to that agent. In addition, agents’ information needs may overlap, so the same data can influence multiple agents simultaneously through spillovers.

The model should be interpreted dynamically. The potential-effect function P(Y,A)(n) describes the ecosystem after n dataflows have taken place. Each dataflow changes the allocation of data across agents and therefore alters the ecosystem’s potential effect. Because the value of data depends on what other data is already available, earlier dataflows can shape the effects of later ones.

These mechanisms imply that data ecosystems need not evolve smoothly: Effects change non-linearly; effects can compound; synergies can appear only after particular combinations of data arrive; and uneven cost structures can concentrate data. In this sense, data ecosystems exhibit the hallmarks of complex systems, in which localized contributions give rise to system-wide effects through interdependence and spillovers. Making these baseline dynamics explicit is important, because interventions, whether regulatory, economic, or technical, do not operate on a static system but instead redirect trajectories that would otherwise unfold on their own. The intervention-free model therefore provides a reference point for analyzing how different interventions alter dataflows and, with them, ecosystem outcomes.

Designing with Data Ecology

A central motivation for data ecology is to inform the design of data ecosystems. In practice, ecosystems are rarely left untouched: Legal rules, technical systems, economic incentives, and social norms continually influence how data moves among agents. From a data ecology perspective, these mechanisms can be understood as interventions, actions, or constraints that redirect dataflows and thereby reshape the allocation of data and its potential effects.

In this section, we use the framework developed in the previous two sections to analyze interventions. We first reinterpret familiar mechanisms as ways of reshaping dataflows to illustrate interventions as a unifying lens. We then derive several structural implications of the data ecology model and examine how these properties shape the effectiveness and limitations of interventions.

Interventions are mechanisms that affect dataflows.  What distinguishes interventions is not their disciplinary origin but rather how they reshape dataflows. Reinterpreting existing mechanisms in this way reveals commonalities among approaches that are often studied in isolation. This shift provides a common basis for comparing mechanisms from different disciplines that would otherwise appear incommensurable.

Some interventions regulate who can access data and under what conditions. Encryption, for example, alters document accessibility by making dataflows effectively free for agents with the appropriate keys and prohibitively costly for others.7 Subscription models, confidentiality rules in professional settings, and consent frameworks operate similarly, restricting dataflows by specifying who is authorized to access particular documents. Although these mechanisms arise from different domains, they intervene on ecosystems in the same structural way: by selectively blocking or enabling dataflows.

Other interventions constrain what data can reveal, even when dataflows occur. Differential privacy limits the inferences that can be drawn from a dataset by deliberately reducing the information it reveals.13 Purpose-limitation and data-minimization policies play a similar role, restricting the tasks for which data may be used rather than whether it may be shared. These interventions reshape ecosystems not by stopping dataflows outright but rather by attenuating their downstream effects.

A third class of interventions reshapes dataflows by making them conditional or staged. Data escrows, for example, allow parties to evaluate the potential effect of a dataflow without revealing the underlying data itself, enabling forms of sharing that would otherwise be too risky.31,39 Related proposals, including in-situ data rights,38 data collaboratives,21 and data unions,30 seek to expand the space of feasible dataflows by changing when, how, and by whom data can be accessed.

Taken together, these examples illustrate how seemingly disparate mechanisms can be understood as interventions on dataflows. Rather than categorizing interventions according to institutional form or policy intent, data ecology focuses attention on how they reshape dataflows in an ecosystem.

The data ecology potential-effect function provides a basis for analyzing the consequences of such interventions. In particular, it highlights several structural properties of data ecosystems that shape both the opportunities and the limits of such interventions, as we discuss next.

Structural implications of the data ecology potential-effect function.  The potential-effct function implies several structural properties of data ecosystems. The following propositions highlight how the model’s components—dataflows, value of data, spillovers, and processing costs—shape ecosystem dynamics.

Proposition 1: Data’s effect on ecosystems depends on dataflows.  The potential effect of data in an ecosystem depends on how data is allocated across agents, which in turn depends on the dataflows that have occurred.

Model mechanism. The ecosystem’s potential effect depends on the value of each agent’s data Bi(n) to solve tasks. Because dataflows determine Bi(n) in this dynamical system, they impact data’s potential effect in the ecosystem.

Implications. Interventions influence ecosystem outcomes by altering dataflows. Dataflows that occur, and those that do not, can both have important consequences; for example, restricting access to medical records may prevent harmful misuse but may also prevent beneficial research. Conversely, enabling new forms of data sharing may unlock new capabilities while also introducing new risks.

Proposition 2: Spillovers are structurally unavoidable.  Dataflows affect agents beyond those directly involved in the exchange.

Model mechanism. Because states of nature are correlated, data about one entity can reveal data about others. The potential-effect function explicitly includes spillover terms V(Y–[i];Bi), reflecting how one agent’s data can affect other agents’ information needs.

Implications. Spillovers complicate governance because the effects of sharing data are rarely confined to the agents who share it. As a result, governance mechanisms that rely primarily on individual data rights may fail to account for the broader ecosystem effects of dataflows.

Even without exchange, spillovers (due to data correlations) make it difficult to classify datasets as intrinsically “sensitive” or “non-sensitive,” rendering interventions that rely on such distinctions ineffective.

Proposition 3: Data ecosystems exhibit path dependence.  Early dataflows can influence long-run ecosystem outcomes by shaping both future data value and future processing costs.

Model mechanism. In the model, each agent’s data Bi(n) evolves with the sequence of dataflows, and processing costs β(n) may depend on the mix of documents an agent has previously integrated. Because the value of data is combinatorial, earlier dataflows affect the value of later ones.

Implications. Path dependence implies that early advantages can compound over time. Agents that gain early access to valuable data may become increasingly capable of generating further insights, reinforcing their position within the ecosystem. This dynamic is visible in domains ranging from digital platforms to machine-learning development, where access to early datasets can shape long-term technological trajectories.

Proposition 4: Integration asymmetries produce hubs.  Agents with greater capacity to process documents tend to become hubs that accumulate and integrate dataflows from many sources.

Model mechanism. Agents with lower processing costs will extract more value from data than those with higher processing costs. Path dependence compounds these effects over time. Another compounding effect is data’s combinatorial value, which may further decrease the cost of processing future documents.

Implications. Data hubs often emerge even without deliberate design. Agents with strong computational infrastructure, specialized expertise, or privileged access to data may become central points of data aggregation. Interventions that focus on breaking hubs may be ineffective if they overlook the structural factors that generate data hubs.

Conclusion: Shaping Data Ecosystems

Data is everywhere. It flows not only through digital infrastructure and institutional databases, but also through biological systems, social rituals, cultural traditions, and algorithmic platforms. It encodes genomes, habits, preferences, and predictions. And because it moves so widely, it influences outcomes not just for those who generate it, but also for entire populations of possibly unaware agents, sometimes across time and generations.

In this article, we propose an initial model of data ecology: a framework for understanding how data shapes ecosystems. By distinguishing data from documents, separating instrumental value from value judgment, and modeling dataflows explicitly, the framework captures mechanisms by which data propagates, accumulates, and transforms systems.

The model shows that the potential effect of data arises through dataflows. These dataflows are shaped by agents’ skills, preferences, and constraints, as well as by technical, economic, and legal interventions. Yet potential effect is not always realized: Costs, capabilities, and power determine whether value materializes, and for whom. Seeing ecosystems in this way allows us to evaluate interventions based on their effect on dataflows.

Modern AI systems make these dynamics especially visible. LLMs, for example, appear as single entities, yet their behavior reflects a dense ecosystem of human contributions, curated documents, fine-tuning signals, and feedback loops. Interacting with such models is, in a sense, interacting with a distributed cultural artifact—an accumulation of stories, abstractions, and inferences shaped by millions of contributors. Data ecology offers a vocabulary for understanding these systems not as monoliths, but as evolving ecosystems whose behavior emerges from the dataflows that sustain them.

As data ecosystems grow more complex and consequential, the need for principled design increases. Data ecology provides a way to see structure where complexity obscures it and to reason coherently across technical, economic, legal, and social domains. Whether the goal is enabling safe sharing, preserving autonomy, ensuring fairness, or unlocking scientific insight, shaping data ecosystems requires understanding how data produces outcomes. Data ecology offers that understanding, and with it, the foundation for designing ecosystems that are fit for the complexity of the world they shape.

item.title: AI Agents Need an Undo Button
item.dc:creator: Tanmay Sah
item.description: As agents gain the ability to modify persistent state, the problem is no longer only whether the model can reason correctly, but whether we can recover from the consequences when it does not.
item.content:encoded:
For many of us, the first real encounter with generative AI came with ChatGPT.1 We gave the model an input, and it generated an output.

One limitation was that the model could not reliably answer questions about information it had not learned during training. Two approaches became especially important for extending these capabilities: fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. Fine-tuning adapts a model using additional training data, while RAG connects the model to external knowledge sources.2 That connection to external knowledge later became part of a broader capability: tool calling. Instead of only generating text, an LLM can determine which tool should be used and generate the arguments needed to call it, whether that tool retrieves information, queries a database, executes code, or invokes an external API.3 Tool calling significantly expanded what LLMs could do and helped lead to agents, which we can think of as an LLM operating inside a harness that provides tools, state, memory, context, and execution logic. This shifts the interaction from simply asking for an answer to giving the system a goal and allowing it to take actions toward that goal.

Agents now come in several forms, including self-evolving coding agents that can modify parts of their framework, memory, skills, tools, models, or collaboration structures.4

The Problem We Face

As agents are given more autonomy, their failures become more consequential. An incorrect answer can often be ignored or regenerated; an incorrect action can change real system state. An agent may call the wrong tool, use incorrect arguments, act on stale information, repeat an operation after losing an acknowledgement, complete only part of a multi-step workflow, or make a locally reasonable change that causes problems later. These risks become even greater when agents operate for longer horizons or modify their own prompts, tools, files, configurations, or code, because one harmful change can influence many later decisions. As agents gain the ability to modify persistent state, the problem is therefore no longer only whether the model can reason correctly, but whether we can recover from the consequences when it does not.6

How We Can Solve It

Verification. One way to reduce these failures is through verification: before an agent takes a consequential action, we check whether the proposed action is valid, safe, and consistent with the goal. Verification can include checking tool arguments, validating code before execution, testing whether an action violates a policy, or using another model or deterministic verifier to inspect the proposed step. In our Verifier Tax work,5 we studied 2,970 agent trajectories and found that verification can improve safety, but it also comes with costs in computation, token usage, and sometimes task success. Verification is therefore an important safeguard, but we should not assume it will catch every failure before it happens.

Recovery. That is why recovery is the other half of the solution. If verification asks, “Should the agent do this?”, recovery asks, “What happens if it already did?” Once an agent changes a database, modifies code, calls an external API, or alters its own tools or prompts, we need a way to understand what changed and, when possible, return the system to a safe state. Our work on EvoUndo6 explores this idea by making changes explicit, preserving the information needed for recovery, and verifying whether a modification can be safely recovered from across different states. We have also released a public implementation of EvoUndo that provides state recoverability, crash reconciliation, and selective undo for autonomous agents that modify external state.7 The goal is not to prevent every possible mistake, but to ensure that a mistake does not automatically become an irreversible failure.

The Path Forward

As agents become more capable and are trusted with more consequential actions, we should not design them around the assumption that every mistake can be prevented. Reliable software systems have always combined prevention with recovery, and agentic systems should do the same. Verification helps us reduce harmful actions before they happen, while recovery limits the damage when prevention fails. Together, they give us a more practical foundation for trustworthy autonomy: not agents that never fail, but systems that can detect, contain, and recover from failure when it happens.

Disclosure: We used AI for editing.

References

1. OpenAI. Introducing ChatGPT, November 30, 2022. https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/

2. Lewis, P., Perez, E., Piktus, A., et al. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020).

3. Schick, T., Dwivedi-Yu, J., Dessì, R., et al. Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2023).

4. Zhou, H., Hu, H., Shang, Y., and Zhang, Q. Self-Evolving Coding Agents, arXiv:2608.03392 (2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03392

5. Sah, T., Srivastava, V., Sah, D., and Jordan, K. The Verifier Tax: Horizon Dependent Safety-Success Tradeoffs in Tool Using LLM Agents., Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (CAIS ’26), 785–799 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3786335.3813160

6. Sah, T., Sah, D., Jain, H., and Sah, T. EvoUndo: Recoverability-Constrained Self-Evolution for LLM Agent Harnesses, arXiv:2608.28363 (2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28363

7. EvoUndo. EvoUndo, GitHub repository (2026). https://github.com/evoundo/evoundo
